topic-160-a-closer-look-at-accuracy-vs-r.evolution: The collection includes a 1990 examination of connection damage, followed by constraints-based robustness measures and scalable defenses. Later work exposes robust overfitting and analyzes local geometry. Recent backdoor results examine stronger adversaries and gaps between robust teachers and students. These findings complicate simple claims that sparsity, scale, or longer training automatically improve security.
openQuestions: How can robust evaluation detect training-specific overfitting?
Which trust assumptions remain necessary when model providers themselves may be adversarial?
topic-160-a-closer-look-at-accuracy-vs-r.overview: This topic investigates how neural networks respond to input attacks, damaged connections, altered weights, and malicious training. It combines empirical studies of robust generalization with certificates and impossibility results. The threat model matters: resistance to small input changes is different from detecting a backdoor inserted by the trainer.
topic-160-a-closer-look-at-accuracy-vs-r.title: Neural Robustness, Generalization, and Hidden Vulnerabilities
topic-160-a-closer-look-at-accuracy-vs-r.whyItMatters: A defense can appear strong on training attacks yet overfit and lose robustness on new examples. Conversely, limits on detecting maliciously trained models show why inspecting weights alone may not establish trust under every adversary.

topic-161-s-3-increasing-gpu-utilization.evolution: An early representative analyzes dataflow architectures for neural simulation. Recent work concentrates on large-language-model serving, including commodity-GPU offloading, dynamic pipeline redistribution, and on-device mixture-of-experts execution. The continuing theme is matching computation to the memory and communication hierarchy, while modern workloads add much larger state and changing request patterns.
openQuestions: Which scheduling policies remain effective under unpredictable multi-model demand?
How should comparisons separate throughput gains from increased per-request latency?
topic-161-s-3-increasing-gpu-utilization.overview: Large-model efficiency depends on moving and scheduling data as much as on arithmetic. These papers study offloading across memory tiers, pipeline parallelism, expert caching, prewarming, and speculative execution. The right arrangement depends on hardware constraints and whether the workload prioritizes response latency or total throughput.
topic-161-s-3-increasing-gpu-utilization.title: Memory Management and Scheduling for Large-Model Systems
topic-161-s-3-increasing-gpu-utilization.whyItMatters: A model that does not fit in accelerator memory can still run by exploiting other storage, but transfers may become the bottleneck. Good systems coordinate compression, caching, and batching instead of optimizing each component independently.

topic-162-i-mind-insightful-multi-subjec.evolution: Early examples represent part–whole hierarchies with bottom-up and top-down pathways. Later work compares task-derived networks with cortical responses and reconstructs images from activity. Recent models use few-shot in-context adaptation and large-scale fMRI pretraining; benchmark null results on trait prediction provide an important counterweight to success on cognitive-state decoding.
openQuestions: Which representational similarities predict useful transfer to unseen subjects?
How can models distinguish genuine neural structure from acquisition-specific regularities?
topic-162-i-mind-insightful-multi-subjec.overview: This topic links artificial visual representations with brain activity, studying both brain-inspired computation and models that predict recorded neural responses. Hierarchical structure, recurrence, predictive feedback, and transfer across subjects appear throughout the representatives. Similarity to brain measurements is an empirical target, not evidence that two systems implement the same mechanism.
topic-162-i-mind-insightful-multi-subjec.title: Visual Cortex Models and Brain-Aligned Representations
topic-162-i-mind-insightful-multi-subjec.whyItMatters: Cross-subject transfer can reduce expensive data collection, while controlled comparisons reveal which aspects of neural activity a model actually captures. Strong visual decoding does not necessarily imply accurate prediction of stable individual traits.

topic-163-3d-steerable-cnns-learning-rot.evolution: The representatives span constrained higher-order networks in 1987, learned invariants, and later group-based geometric models. Recent work combines learned canonicalization, approximate equivariance, and applications such as rotation-invariant spherical watermarking. These examples broaden the transformations and data spaces considered while retaining the need to specify the group action precisely.
openQuestions: How should models handle ambiguous canonical frames without unstable predictions?
When is approximate symmetry more useful than an exact architectural constraint?
topic-163-3d-steerable-cnns-learning-rot.overview: Symmetry-aware learning makes outputs transform predictably when inputs rotate, translate, or undergo another structured change. Some methods constrain the architecture; others first map inputs into a learned canonical frame. The appropriate choice depends on whether a transformation should preserve the answer or change it in a known way.
topic-163-3d-steerable-cnns-learning-rot.title: Symmetry, Equivariance, and Canonical Representations
topic-163-3d-steerable-cnns-learning-rot.whyItMatters: Encoding a valid symmetry can reduce redundant learning, but enforcing the wrong one can remove useful information. Canonicalization also introduces its own ambiguity when several orientations or configurations are equally plausible.

topic-164-a-federated-stochastic-multi-l.evolution: The 2017 multi-task perspective explicitly considers systems heterogeneity. Subsequent work develops drift correction and arbitrary communication patterns, followed by compressed adaptive methods and stronger participation guarantees. Recent approaches combine parameter-free updates, error feedback, and resource-adaptive fine-tuning. The evidence suggests several ways to reduce coordination costs, each tied to assumptions about sampling and heterogeneity.
openQuestions: How can guarantees remain useful when participation correlates with client data?
When do communication savings outweigh the bias introduced by longer local training?
topic-164-a-federated-stochastic-multi-l.overview: Federated optimization trains across clients whose data, availability, and computing resources differ. The represented methods reduce communication, correct local-update drift, adapt optimization, and account for partial participation. These are coupled problems because saving synchronization can amplify differences between clients.
topic-164-a-federated-stochastic-multi-l.title: Federated Optimization under Heterogeneity and Communication Constraints
topic-164-a-federated-stochastic-multi-l.whyItMatters: Keeping data local does not make distributed optimization simple or automatically private. Practical performance requires methods that tolerate slow devices and uneven sampling while preserving the intended statistical objective.

topic-165-2d-conditional-random-fields-f.evolution: The historical examples include parallel parsers in the late 1980s and shared-context transducers in 1997. Later papers learn constituent and dependency structure. A recent controlled grammar study connects cross-scale correlations with the emergence of hierarchical neural representations. This provides a testable mechanism in a simplified setting, not a complete explanation of natural-language acquisition.
openQuestions: Which language statistics support hierarchy rather than surface pattern matching?
How do findings from controlled grammars transfer to noisy, heterogeneous natural text?
topic-165-2d-conditional-random-fields-f.overview: This topic studies how linguistic structure can be learned and represented, from probabilistic transducers to grammar induction and neural parsing. Local word statistics must support relationships that span larger phrases and nested constructions. Compact parameter sharing and contextual information help models generalize beyond memorized strings.
topic-165-2d-conditional-random-fields-f.title: Grammar Learning and Hierarchical Language Structure
topic-165-2d-conditional-random-fields-f.whyItMatters: A system may predict nearby words accurately while failing to recover the hierarchical organization needed for compositional understanding. Tractable language models make it possible to test which statistics support that organization and how ambiguity affects learning.

topic-166-canonical-tensor-decomposition.evolution: The collection includes early factor-analysis and nonnegative-factorization work, then subspace, sparse, and tensor-train methods. Later results sharpen completion guarantees and online algorithms. Recent dual-spectral regularization distinguishes sparsity across frequencies from low rank within them, while tensor networks support graph and explanation applications. These developments refine which structure is preserved rather than simply reducing every dimension equally.
openQuestions: Which rank or sparsity assumptions can be diagnosed from incomplete data?
How can scalable algorithms retain guarantees under noisy and non-Gaussian observations?
topic-166-canonical-tensor-decomposition.overview: Tensors organize data across several interacting axes, such as entities, time, channels, or relations. Low-rank decompositions aim to exploit that structure for compact representation and recovery of missing entries. Different factorization families encode different assumptions, so tensor rank is not a single interchangeable quantity.
topic-166-canonical-tensor-decomposition.title: Tensor Factorization and Structured Multiway Data
topic-166-canonical-tensor-decomposition.whyItMatters: Scalability and statistical reliability must be considered together. A representation can save memory yet remain hard to fit, and a uniform regularizer can miss differences between frequency components or modes.

topic-167-a-general-theory-for-softmax-g.evolution: Early representatives use expectation-maximization for incomplete data and diagnostic mixtures. Later work develops mixture hierarchies and analyzes optimization in Gaussian mixtures. Recent approaches connect diffusion objectives, semidefinite relaxations, and moment-based distribution approximation. This expands the inference tools available, while global guarantees remain conditional on properties such as parameter constraints and rank conditions.
openQuestions: When do finite moments determine a useful mixing distribution?
How can model selection avoid adding components that merely absorb noise or missing-data artifacts?
topic-167-a-general-theory-for-softmax-g.overview: Mixture models describe a distribution as a combination of simpler components, allowing heterogeneous populations to be represented without forcing one global shape. Learning must determine component parameters, mixing weights, and sometimes the number of components. Missing or quantized observations add further ambiguity.
topic-167-a-general-theory-for-softmax-g.title: Mixture Models and Latent Population Structure
topic-167-a-general-theory-for-softmax-g.whyItMatters: An apparent cluster can depend strongly on the assumed component family and optimization procedure. Useful methods need both computational strategies and conditions explaining when the latent structure is identifiable or reliably approximated.
